content.text:
If you’re in the **United States**, you probably **can’t legally buy a true Japanese dwarf flying squirrel** (*Pteromys momonga*) as a pet. They’re a wild species native to Japan, and I’m not seeing legitimate U.S. pet-market sources for captive-bred Japanese dwarf flying squirrels. Be very cautious of online listings—many are scams or illegal wildlife trade.

What you can do instead:

1. **Check your state wildlife agency first**  
   Flying-squirrel ownership rules vary a lot by state, and permits may be required. Some states ban them entirely. ([legalclarity.org](https://legalclarity.org/is-it-legal-to-own-a-flying-squirrel/?utm_source=openai))

2. **If legal where you live, look for a USDA-licensed breeder of captive-bred flying squirrels**  
   In the U.S., the species typically sold as a pet is the **southern flying squirrel**, not the Japanese dwarf flying squirrel. Reputable sellers should provide a USDA license number, captive-bred documentation, and health records. ([legalclarity.org](https://legalclarity.org/is-it-legal-to-own-a-flying-squirrel/?utm_source=openai))

3. **Avoid wild-caught animals or overseas “import” offers**  
   Importing live animals into the U.S. can require permits and health documentation, and illegally sourced wildlife can create serious legal problems. USDA APHIS handles regulated live-animal import requirements. ([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/live-animal-import/frequently-asked-questions-regulated-live-animal-imports?utm_source=openai))

4. **Consider legal alternatives**  
   Depending on your state, you might be able to legally keep a **southern flying squirrel** or possibly a **sugar glider** from a reputable breeder. They still require specialized nocturnal care and an exotic vet.

If you tell me **what state you’re in**, I can help you check whether flying squirrels are legal there and what agency/permit page to start with.
